Central Washington University launches Behavioral Health BS to address workforce needs
Central Washington University has introduced its Behavioral Health Bachelor of Science program this fall to meet increasing demand for mental health professionals statewide. The new degree prepares graduates for key support roles under clinical supervision without requiring immediate entry into graduate school.
Central Washington University began offering a new Bachelor of Science in Behavioral Health this fall, aiming to help psychology majors start careers in the field without first enrolling in graduate school, according to an Oct. 14 announcement.
The Department of Psychology launched the program to address growing industry demand and increased student interest. Psychology Department Chair Heidi Perez said the state Department of Health established a behavioral health support specialist certification in January 2025 due to rising demand for mental health professionals. “Our students have been interested in this type of applied degree for a long time, and the conversation has always been, ‘what can students do with a degree in psychology?’” Perez said. “They can do a lot, but it can be difficult to build a career in psychology without a master’s degree. So we started talking about creating a new degree program to meet that need on the part of students.”
Perez said faculty members developed the curriculum by working with University of Washington implementation guidelines and state rules as well as internal processes at Central Washington University. She added that while similar programs exist statewide, her department identified opportunities for their own program after reviewing evolving requirements. “There are a number of similar programs around the state that are already approved through the Department of Health, but as our faculty group started digging into it, more and more information started coming out and we identified some opportunities to help our program stand out,” she said.
Lecturer Cindy Myers joined full-time faculty in fall 2025 and began recruiting for this quarter’s initial cohort of seven students—many previously enrolled as psychology majors at Central Washington University. Myers participated on a state task force in 2021 examining ways to increase mental health providers statewide. “Ever since COVID, there's been a shortage of mental health counselors in Washington state and across the country, and a lot of people have left the field,” Myers said.
Myers explained that graduates will be certified for tasks such as initial patient intake evaluations, screenings and assessments under supervision from licensed clinicians like herself. “They can do brief interventions, they can co-lead groups, they can provide psychoeducation, and they can do some case management tasks,” she said.
Perez noted that students may double-major or add behavioral health expertise before entering professional roles; currently offered only at the Ellensburg campus but with plans for expansion.
